investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why does ¹⁸F-FDG accumulate in malignant cells?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: FDG is a glucose analogue taken up via GLUT transporters (upregulated in cancer) and phosphorylated by hexokinase to FDG-6-phosphate, which cannot be metabolised further or dephosphorylated, so it becomes metabolically trapped in proportion to glycolytic rate.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the SUV and what is it used for?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The standardised uptake value is a semi-quantitative measure of tracer activity normalised to injected dose and body weight. SUVmax helps characterise lesions and assess treatment response but is not diagnostic on its own.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: List the key patient-preparation steps before FDG PET-CT.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Fast for at least 6 hours, control blood glucose (ideally <11 mmol/L), rest quietly and stay warm during the ~60 min uptake period, and avoid strenuous exercise for 24 h beforehand.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Name common sites of physiological FDG uptake that can mimic pathology.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Brain, myocardium, renal collecting system/ureters/bladder (excretion), bowel, brown fat (neck/supraclavicular/paravertebral) and skeletal muscle.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which tumours characteristically show low or absent FDG uptake (false negatives)?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Low-grade/indolent tumours, mucinous and lepidic adenocarcinomas, well-differentiated HCC, prostate cancer and renal cell carcinoma; also lesions below scanner resolution (sub-centimetre).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why is dietary preparation essential before cardiac FDG-PET?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Normal myocardium avidly takes up glucose (and therefore FDG), masking pathology. A prolonged high-fat, low/zero-carbohydrate diet followed by a fast (± IV heparin) switches myocytes to free-fatty-acid metabolism, suppressing physiological uptake so inflammatory/infective foci become visible.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What FDG pattern suggests active cardiac sarcoidosis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Focal or focal-on-diffuse patchy FDG uptake not respecting coronary territories. Combined with a rest perfusion study, a perfusion–metabolism mismatch (reduced perfusion + increased FDG) indicates active, potentially reversible inflammation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How does FDG-PET feature in the diagnosis of prosthetic-valve endocarditis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Abnormal FDG uptake around the prosthetic valve is a major criterion in the ESC-modified Duke criteria for prosthetic-valve endocarditis. FDG-PET/CT also detects lead, generator-pocket, vascular-graft and metastatic septic foci.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the main cause of a non-diagnostic cardiac FDG-PET, and the chief false positive?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Inadequate dietary suppression leaving residual physiological myocardial uptake is the commonest cause of a non-diagnostic study. Recent cardiac surgery or device implantation causes post-operative inflammatory FDG uptake, a key false positive.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the mechanism and approximate radiation dose of FDG-PET/CT?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: 18F-FDG is a glucose analogue taken up by GLUT transporters, phosphorylated and trapped in metabolically active cells. A typical FDG-PET/CT delivers roughly 6–10 mSv (tracer plus CT); standard pregnancy/breastfeeding precautions apply.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is PSMA and why is it a good imaging target in prostate cancer?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Prostate-specific membrane antigen is a transmembrane glycoprotein (glutamate carboxypeptidase II) overexpressed on prostate cancer cells, with expression rising with higher grade and stage. Radiolabelled ligands bind and are internalised, giving high tumour-to-background contrast.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Name the two common PSMA PET radiotracers and a key difference.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁶⁸Ga-PSMA-11 (gallium-68, half-life ~68 min, generator-produced, imaged locally) and ¹⁸F-DCFPyL (fluorine-18, half-life ~110 min, cyclotron-produced, allowing distribution and higher resolution).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What are the two main clinical indications for PSMA PET?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: High-risk primary staging (detecting nodal/bone metastases with higher sensitivity than CT and bone scan) and biochemical recurrence after treatment (localising disease at low PSA when conventional imaging is negative).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: List common sites of physiological PSMA uptake that can be misread.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Salivary and lacrimal glands, kidneys and ureters, liver and spleen, small bowel, and the urinary bladder (excreted tracer). Coeliac/sympathetic ganglia are a classic false-positive pitfall.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How does PSMA PET link to theranostics?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The same PSMA target used for ⁶⁸Ga/¹⁸F imaging is targeted therapeutically by ¹⁷⁷Lu-PSMA, a beta-emitting radioligand therapy. A PSMA-avid scan confirms the target and selects patients for treatment.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What receptor does ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE bind, and on what tumours is it overexpressed?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It binds somatostatin receptors, chiefly SSTR2, which are overexpressed on well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours (NETs).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which older scan has ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT largely replaced, and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ¹¹¹In-Octreotide (OctreoScan) SPECT. DOTATATE PET offers higher SSTR2 affinity, better spatial resolution, greater sensitivity and a same-day study.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why and how are somatostatin analogues managed before a DOTATATE scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Octreotide/lanreotide compete for SSTR and can cause false-negatives. Withhold short-acting octreotide ~24h before; scan long-acting depot just before the next dose (~3–4 weeks after the last).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: List the sites of physiological ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE uptake.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Spleen (usually most intense), adrenals, pituitary, kidneys/urinary tract, liver, and the uncinate process of the pancreas (a classic pseudolesion).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How do DOTATATE and FDG-PET differ across NET grades?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Well-differentiated low-grade NETs are DOTATATE-avid but FDG-negative. High-grade/poorly-differentiated NETs lose SSTR and become FDG-avid but DOTATATE-negative — the flip-flop phenomenon.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the physical basis of SPECT and its key advantage over planar imaging?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A gamma camera rotates 360° around the patient, and projections are reconstructed into 3D tomographic slices of a single-photon emitter (usually ⁹⁹ᵐTc). This removes structure overlap, and SPECT/CT hybrids add anatomical localisation and attenuation correction.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Mechanism of localisation of ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP on a bone scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: MDP (methylene diphosphonate) adsorbs onto hydroxyapatite at sites of active bone turnover, so uptake reflects osteoblastic activity and regional blood flow — highlighting mets, fractures, Paget's and infection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is a 'superscan' and the 'flare phenomenon'?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Superscan: diffuse intense skeletal uptake with faint/absent kidney and bladder activity, from widespread osteoblastic mets or metabolic bone disease. Flare: apparent worsening of hot spots early after effective treatment, representing healing (osteoblastic) response, not progression.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What tracer is used for a HIDA scan and how does it work?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled iminodiacetic acid analogue — taken up by hepatocytes and excreted unchanged into bile, mapping the biliary tree in real time from liver to duodenum.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What HIDA finding indicates acute cholecystitis, and what other indications exist?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Non-filling of the gallbladder at 60 min (cystic duct obstruction) despite tracer reaching the bowel. HIDA is also used for suspected bile leak (post-cholecystectomy) and neonatal biliary atresia (hepatic uptake but no bowel activity).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which bone-avid tracers are used to image cardiac ATTR, and where?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DPD (UK/Europe), ⁹⁹ᵐTc-PYP (US), and ⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMDP. All are bone-seeking diphosphonate/pyrophosphate tracers that bind amyloid microcalcification in ATTR-infiltrated myocardium.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why does the scan distinguish ATTR from AL amyloidosis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Bone-avid tracers show intense myocardial uptake in ATTR but characteristically little or none in AL. AL can occasionally take up tracer, so a monoclonal protein screen is still mandatory before diagnosing ATTR.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Describe the Perugini visual grading scale.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Grade 0 = no cardiac uptake (negative); Grade 1 = cardiac < bone (equivocal); Grade 2 = cardiac = bone (positive); Grade 3 = cardiac > bone with reduced bone signal (positive). Grade 2–3 is positive for ATTR.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What must be checked BEFORE a positive scan can be called ATTR?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Exclusion of AL amyloid with serum free light chains (normal kappa:lambda ratio) plus serum AND urine immunofixation (no monoclonal band). Any abnormality mandates haematology referral and biopsy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which clinical features should prompt bone scintigraphy for ATTR?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Unexplained LVH/HFpEF in an older patient, low-voltage ECG despite a thick-walled ventricle (voltage–mass mismatch), and a history of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, or biceps tendon rupture.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which radiopharmaceutical is used in three-phase bone scintigraphy and how does it localise?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled diphosphonate (MDP). It is chemisorbed onto hydroxyapatite crystal at sites of active osteoblastic bone mineralisation, so uptake reflects local bone turnover and blood flow.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Name the three phases and their timing.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: 1) Flow/angiographic — dynamic over the first ~60s (blood flow). 2) Blood-pool/soft-tissue — immediate static at ~5 min (hyperaemia). 3) Delayed bone phase — static at 2–4h (osteoblastic uptake).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How does osteomyelitis differ from cellulitis on a three-phase scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Osteomyelitis is positive (focal increased uptake) in all three phases. Cellulitis increases flow and blood-pool activity but shows no focal uptake on the delayed bone phase — the delayed phase is the key discriminator.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: When is three-phase bone scintigraphy least specific, and what helps?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Specificity falls with recent surgery, fracture, orthopaedic metalwork or a neuropathic (Charcot) joint, all of which raise bone turnover. A labelled white-cell scan (⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO or ¹¹¹In leucocytes), often with a marrow study, improves specificity.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Give the main safety points for ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP bone scintigraphy.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Effective dose is a few mSv. Avoid in pregnancy unless justified; minimise close contact and follow local guidance if breastfeeding. Hydrate and void frequently to lower bladder radiation dose.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which radiopharmaceutical is preferred for a dynamic renogram and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAG3 — it is actively secreted by the proximal tubules with high extraction, giving superior image quality, especially in kidneys with poor function. ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA (glomerular filtration) is the alternative.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What does the F+20 / frusemide diuretic renogram distinguish?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: True mechanical obstruction (rising curve that does NOT wash out after diuretic) from a baggy, dilated but non-obstructed system (prompt washout after frusemide).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Describe the normal renogram curve.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A rapid rise (uptake), a peak at about 3–5 minutes, then a steady fall as tracer is excreted and drains to the bladder.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why is captopril used in renography, and what does a positive study show?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Captopril (an ACE inhibitor) unmasks a functionally significant renal artery stenosis. A positive study shows worsening of the affected kidney's curve after captopril — delayed time-to-peak, delayed excretion and reduced relative uptake versus baseline.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Name two patient-prep factors that can cause a false non-washout (false obstruction) pattern.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Dehydration (slows tracer transit) and a full bladder causing back-pressure — so hydrate the patient and have them void before imaging.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the mechanism of localisation of ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DMSA?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It is taken up and fixed in proximal renal tubular cells of the cortex, with minimal collecting-system excretion, so uptake maps functioning cortical mass.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why is DMSA the best test for split renal function and scarring?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Because retained cortical tracer directly reflects viable functioning parenchyma, giving high-resolution cortical images and accurate differential (split) function without pelvicalyceal activity obscuring the cortex.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How do you distinguish acute pyelonephritis from a chronic scar on DMSA?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Acute pyelonephritis shows photopenic (cold) defects with a preserved renal outline and no volume loss; a scar shows a focal defect with cortical thinning/volume loss, classically wedge-shaped.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: When should scarring be assessed on DMSA relative to an acute UTI?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Delayed several months (usually at least 4–6 months) after the acute infection, so acute inflammatory change is not mistaken for a permanent scar.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: When is DMSA imaging performed after injection, and what is a normal split function?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Imaging is performed about 2–4 hours after IV injection; normal split function is roughly symmetrical, around 45–55% per kidney.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How does ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate localise in the thyroid, and what is its key limitation?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It is trapped by the sodium-iodide symporter but NOT organified. It therefore reflects trapping only and cannot assess organification defects (unlike radioiodine).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Thyrotoxic patient with diffuse, homogeneously increased tracer uptake across an enlarged gland — diagnosis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Graves' disease.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Single hot nodule with suppressed uptake in the surrounding gland — diagnosis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Toxic (autonomously functioning) adenoma.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Thyrotoxic patient with near-absent thyroid uptake — differential?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Thyroiditis (de Quervain's, silent/post-partum), factitious thyrotoxicosis, iodine load, or recent amiodarone.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What does a COLD (hypofunctioning) nodule imply and what is the next step?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A slightly higher malignancy risk than a hot nodule — proceed to ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How does the thyroid concentrate radioiodine, and why does this make iodine isotopes useful both diagnostically and therapeutically?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Follicular cells trap iodide via the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) and organify it into thyroid hormone. Gamma-emitting ¹²³I images this uptake (RAIU), while beta-emitting ¹³¹I delivers a local ablative dose to functioning tissue for therapy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: In a thyrotoxic patient, what do HIGH versus LOW radioiodine uptake indicate?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: High uptake = Graves' disease (diffuse) or toxic nodular disease / toxic adenoma (focal). Low uptake = thyroiditis (subacute, postpartum), iodine load (contrast, amiodarone), or factitious thyroxine ingestion.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Contrast ¹²³I and ¹³¹I in terms of emission, half-life and use.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ¹²³I: pure gamma emitter, ~13 h half-life, low dose — used for diagnostic uptake and imaging. ¹³¹I: beta and gamma emitter, ~8 day half-life — beta particles ablate tissue for therapy of hyperthyroidism and thyroid cancer, and it is used for whole-body scans.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What are the absolute contraindications and key post-therapy precautions for ¹³¹I radioiodine?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Pregnancy and breastfeeding are absolute contraindications (mandatory pregnancy test first). After therapy: keep distance from children and pregnant women, limit close contact, and avoid pregnancy for about 6 months.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why must patients follow a low-iodine diet and stop antithyroid drugs before radioiodine, and what is a risk in Graves' patients?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Iodine loading and antithyroid drugs suppress uptake, reducing efficacy, so both are stopped/avoided beforehand. In Graves' disease, radioiodine can precipitate or worsen thyroid eye disease, especially in smokers, sometimes needing steroid cover.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the purpose of ultrasound guidance during thyroid FNA?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It directs the needle into the most suspicious solid, vascular part of the nodule and avoids cystic/necrotic areas, improving sample adequacy and reducing non-diagnostic (Thy1) results compared with palpation-guided FNA.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What do Thy1 and Thy1c mean, and what is the next step?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Thy1 = non-diagnostic/inadequate; Thy1c = cystic non-diagnostic (acellular cyst fluid). Management is to repeat the US-guided FNA, sampling any solid component.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why can't cytology (Thy3f) distinguish a follicular adenoma from a follicular carcinoma?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The malignant diagnosis depends on capsular and vascular invasion, which is an architectural feature. FNA samples loose cells only, so it cannot assess the capsule — a diagnostic hemithyroidectomy is needed for histology.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What does the BTA 'U' ultrasound classification (U1-U5) represent?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A sonographic risk score: U1 normal, U2 benign, U3 indeterminate, U4 suspicious, U5 malignant. U3-U5 nodules are selected for FNA.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How is a Thy2 benign cytology managed, and what is the key caveat?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Thy2 (non-neoplastic/benign, e.g. colloid nodule) is managed by reassurance and discharge or interval ultrasound. Caveat: a benign result must not override a suspicious ultrasound or clinical features — discordance needs MDT review and re-sampling.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What three tracer properties make an ideal GFR marker, and which isotopes are used?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Freely filtered at the glomerulus, not secreted, and not reabsorbed by the tubules — so plasma clearance equals GFR. UK tracers are ⁵¹Cr-EDTA (chromium-51) or ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Outline the isotope GFR method.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Single accurately-measured IV bolus of tracer, then timed venous blood samples (e.g. 2, 3, 4 h) from the opposite arm. Log plasma activity is plotted against time; the terminal slope/AUC gives clearance, corrected to body surface area (mL/min/1.73m²).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why is isotope GFR preferred over creatinine-based eGFR?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It directly measures filtration of a pure marker rather than estimating from creatinine, which depends on muscle mass. It is the reference/gold-standard when accuracy changes management — chemo dosing, kidney donors, children, and extremes of muscle mass or amputees.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which chemotherapy dosing formula relies on an accurate measured GFR?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The Calvert formula for carboplatin: dose = target AUC × (GFR + 25). An isotope GFR is requested to avoid over- or under-dosing this nephrotoxic drug.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What clinical state most distorts an isotope GFR result, and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Extracellular fluid overload (oedema, ascites): the tracer distributes into the expanded ECF, delaying equilibration and giving an unreliable single-pool result. Extended/multi-sample protocols are needed. Accurate dose and sample timing are also essential.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which two radiopharmaceuticals are used in a V/Q scan and by what route?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Perfusion: IV ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAA (macroaggregated albumin), which lodges in pulmonary capillaries. Ventilation: inhaled ⁹⁹ᵐTc-Technegas or ⁸¹ᵐKr gas reaching the alveoli.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the diagnostic hallmark of PE on a V/Q scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A MISMATCH — a perfusion defect with preserved (normal) ventilation in the same lung region. Matched V and Q defects point to airway/parenchymal disease instead.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: When is a V/Q scan preferred over CTPA?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Suspected PE with a NORMAL chest X-ray in patients where CTPA is contraindicated or best avoided: contrast allergy, renal impairment, or to reduce breast radiation in younger women and pregnancy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What does a normal perfusion scan tell you about PE?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A normal perfusion scan effectively excludes pulmonary embolism.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How is a V/Q scan reported?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: By probability (PIOPED-style): normal, low, intermediate/indeterminate, or high probability. High probability requires large mismatched segmental perfusion defects.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What does uptake of ⁹⁹ᵐTc-sestamibi/tetrofosmin in the myocardium reflect?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Regional coronary blood flow AND myocyte viability — the lipophilic cation is trapped in mitochondria of perfused, living myocytes in proportion to flow.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Reversible vs fixed defect on SPECT MPI — meaning?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Reversible (abnormal on stress, normal at rest) = inducible ischaemia from a flow-limiting stenosis. Fixed (abnormal on both) = infarct/scar (non-viable), though hibernating myocardium can mimic it.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How do vasodilator stress agents (adenosine/dipyridamole/regadenoson) reveal ischaemia?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: They dilate normal coronaries but stenosed vessels are already maximally dilated, creating flow heterogeneity/'coronary steal' so diseased territories show relatively reduced tracer uptake.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Key contraindications and prep for adenosine/dipyridamole MPI stress?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Contraindicated in asthma/bronchospasm and high-grade AV block (no pacemaker). Withhold caffeine and theophylline ≥12–24 h (competitive antagonists causing false negatives). Have resuscitation facilities and aminophylline ready.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which stress agent is preferred when a patient has asthma, and why choose it?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Dobutamine — an inotrope/chronotrope that raises myocardial oxygen demand rather than acting on adenosine receptors, so it avoids the bronchospasm risk of vasodilators.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: By what mechanism does MIBG localise to tumours?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: MIBG is a noradrenaline (norepinephrine) analogue taken up via the noradrenaline transporter into adrenergic/sympathomedullary and neural-crest tissue, then stored in neurosecretory granules.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What are the main indications for an MIBG scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Localising and staging phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma, and neuroblastoma in children; also assessing avidity/suitability for 131I-MIBG therapy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why and how is thyroid blockade given before an MIBG scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Potassium iodide or Lugol's iodine is given before and after the scan to saturate the thyroid and block uptake of free radioiodine, protecting the gland from radiation. Blockade is longer when 131I is used.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which drugs must be withheld before MIBG imaging and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Labetalol (and other combined alpha/beta blockers), tricyclic antidepressants, sympathomimetics/decongestants and some calcium-channel blockers block or displace MIBG at the noradrenaline transporter, causing false-negative scans.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: When are images acquired and what are the normal physiological uptake sites?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Imaging at 24 hours, with delayed 48-hour views if needed, often with SPECT/CT. Physiological uptake: salivary glands, myocardium, liver, spleen, bowel and bladder.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What does ¹²³I-ioflupane (DaTscan) bind, and where?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The presynaptic dopamine transporter (DAT) on nigrostriatal dopaminergic nerve terminals in the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What appearance is normal vs abnormal on a DaTscan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Normal = symmetric crescent/'comma'-shaped uptake in both striata. Abnormal = reduced/asymmetric uptake shrinking to a 'full stop'/period and losing the putaminal tail (presynaptic dopaminergic deficit).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which conditions give a REDUCED DaTscan vs a NORMAL one?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Reduced (degenerative): Parkinson's disease, MSA, PSP, and dementia with Lewy bodies. Normal (intact terminals): essential tremor, drug-induced, vascular and psychogenic parkinsonism.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the key limitation of a DaTscan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It confirms a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit but CANNOT distinguish Parkinson's disease from MSA or PSP, since all degenerative parkinsonian syndromes reduce striatal uptake.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What patient preparation is required before a DaTscan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Thyroid blockade with potassium iodide/perchlorate to protect the thyroid from free radioiodide, and withholding drugs that affect DAT binding (cocaine, some stimulants such as methylphenidate/amfetamine, and certain antidepressants like bupropion). SPECT imaging is performed ~3–6 hours after injection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which radiopharmaceutical is used for labelled RBC scintigraphy in GI bleeding, and where does it localise?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled autologous red blood cells. They remain in the intravascular blood pool; extravasation into the bowel lumen produces an abnormal focus of activity.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the diagnostic hallmark of a positive labelled RBC bleeding scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A focus of activity that appears, increases in intensity, and moves along the bowel with peristalsis on dynamic imaging.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What bleeding rate can labelled RBC scintigraphy detect, and how does this compare to angiography?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: As low as ~0.1–0.4 mL/min — more sensitive than CT angiography or catheter angiography, which need faster bleeding.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Give the main advantage and the main limitation of labelled RBC scintigraphy.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Advantage: prolonged/repeatable imaging window catches slow, intermittent bleeds. Limitation: localises the region but not the exact cause, and peristalsis can mislocalise the source.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How does the Meckel's scan differ from labelled RBC scintigraphy?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It uses free ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate (not RBC-bound), which is taken up by ectopic gastric mucosa in a Meckel's diverticulum — a classic cause of painless PR bleeding in children.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How do labelled white cells localise to infection?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Autologous leucocytes (mainly neutrophils) are labelled ex vivo and reinjected; they marginate, extravasate and accumulate at sites of active neutrophilic inflammation in response to chemotactic signals, so uptake marks active infection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Compare ⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO and ¹¹¹In-oxine for leucocyte labelling.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO gives lower dose and sharper images but shows physiological bowel/urinary/gallbladder clearance on delayed views. ¹¹¹In-oxine is very stable with no bowel excretion (good for abdominal sepsis) but delivers a higher dose with poorer resolution.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why add a bone marrow scan to a labelled WCC scan for prosthetic joint infection?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Normal/displaced marrow takes up leucocytes and can mimic infection. Infection is WCC uptake that is NOT matched on the marrow map (incongruent); congruent uptake is marrow. This co-registration greatly improves specificity.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What imaging pattern over time indicates active infection on a labelled WCC scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A focus of uptake outside the normal liver/spleen/marrow distribution that is stable or increases in intensity and extent between early and delayed images indicates active infection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: List the main indications for a labelled white cell scan.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Suspected osteomyelitis (especially prosthetic joint infection and diabetic foot), infected vascular grafts, occult abdominal/pelvic collections, inflammatory bowel disease activity, and pyrexia/inflammation of unknown origin.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the sentinel lymph node?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The first lymph node (or nodes) into which a tumour drains, and therefore the first likely site of nodal metastasis. Its status is used to predict the state of the whole regional nodal basin.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which radiopharmaceutical is used for sentinel node mapping and how does it localise?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled nanocolloid, injected around the tumour or biopsy site. The small colloid particles enter the lymphatics and are trapped/phagocytosed in the first draining (sentinel) node, making it a focal hot spot on gamma imaging.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is 'dual localisation' in sentinel node biopsy?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Combining the radiotracer (⁹⁹ᵐTc-nanocolloid, found with the gamma probe) with intra-operative blue dye that stains the node and afferent lymphatic blue. Using both raises the sentinel-node identification rate above either method alone.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What do a negative and a positive sentinel node each mean for management?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A negative sentinel node avoids the need for full axillary/regional nodal dissection, sparing the patient its morbidity (lymphoedema). A positive node guides further management such as further nodal treatment, radiotherapy or surveillance.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Name the key safety issues in sentinel node lymphoscintigraphy.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Low radiation dose from the small ⁹⁹ᵐTc activity (safe for patient and staff); risk of anaphylaxis to patent blue dye plus transient blue staining and an artefactual SpO₂ drop; pregnancy is a relative contraindication and breastfeeding may need temporary interruption.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: What is the biochemical basis for ¹⁸F-FDG retention within tumour cells?
options: It binds irreversibly to cell-surface somatostatin receptors
It is phosphorylated to FDG-6-phosphate and trapped intracellularly
It is incorporated into newly synthesised DNA strands
It chelates intracellular calcium in metabolically active cells
It is actively secreted into the biliary system and reabsorbed
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: It is phosphorylated to FDG-6-phosphate and trapped intracellularly
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: FDG enters cells via GLUT transporters and is phosphorylated by hexokinase to FDG-6-phosphate. This charged metabolite cannot progress through glycolysis or be dephosphorylated, so it accumulates in proportion to the cell's glycolytic activity.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient is booked for FDG PET-CT. Which preparation instruction is correct?
options: Perform vigorous exercise on the morning of the scan
Eat a high-carbohydrate meal one hour before injection
Fast for at least 6 hours and ensure blood glucose is controlled
Receive a large intravenous dextrose load before injection
Remain in a cold room during the uptake period
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Fast for at least 6 hours and ensure blood glucose is controlled
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Fasting for at least 6 hours lowers insulin and blood glucose so that tumour cells out-compete normal tissue for FDG. Hyperglycaemia competes with the tracer and degrades image quality, so glucose is ideally kept below 11 mmol/L.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which malignancy is most likely to be FDG PET-negative, limiting the test's sensitivity?
options: High-grade diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Non-small-cell lung carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck
Renal cell carcinoma
Poorly differentiated oesophageal adenocarcinoma
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Renal cell carcinoma
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Renal cell carcinoma characteristically shows low FDG avidity, and urinary excretion of tracer through the renal tract further obscures assessment. The other listed tumours are typically strongly FDG-avid and well demonstrated on PET-CT.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient is booked for cardiac FDG-PET to assess suspected cardiac sarcoidosis. Which preparation is most important to make the study interpretable?
options: Prolonged high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet followed by a fast, sometimes with IV heparin
High-carbohydrate loading in the hour before injection
Oral potassium perchlorate to block thyroid uptake
Full bladder protocol with oral contrast
IV beta-blocker to slow the heart rate
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Prolonged high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet followed by a fast, sometimes with IV heparin
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: This regimen switches myocardial metabolism from glucose to free fatty acids, suppressing physiological FDG uptake. Pathological inflammatory uptake then stands out against a silenced background, making the study diagnostic.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: On a well-suppressed cardiac FDG-PET combined with rest perfusion imaging, which finding best indicates active cardiac sarcoidosis amenable to immunosuppression?
options: A region of reduced perfusion with increased FDG uptake (mismatch)
Uniform diffuse FDG uptake throughout the entire myocardium
Normal perfusion with no myocardial FDG uptake
Matched reduction in both perfusion and FDG uptake
Increased FDG uptake confined to the blood pool
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A region of reduced perfusion with increased FDG uptake (mismatch)
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A perfusion–metabolism mismatch reflects active granulomatous inflammation that is potentially reversible with treatment. A matched perfusion–FDG defect instead indicates established scar, and absent uptake indicates no active disease.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with a prosthetic aortic valve has persistent bacteraemia but an equivocal echocardiogram. FDG-PET/CT shows abnormal uptake around the valve sewing ring. How is this best interpreted?
options: It is a major criterion for prosthetic-valve endocarditis in the ESC-modified Duke criteria
It is a normal finding for any prosthetic valve regardless of timing
It excludes infection and confirms a mechanical valve leak
It is diagnostic only of extracardiac malignancy
It reliably indicates infection even one week after valve surgery
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: It is a major criterion for prosthetic-valve endocarditis in the ESC-modified Duke criteria
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Abnormal FDG uptake around a prosthetic valve is incorporated as a major criterion for prosthetic-valve endocarditis. Interpretation must account for post-operative inflammation, which causes uptake for weeks to months after surgery.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 68-year-old man has a rising PSA of 0.4 ng/mL two years after radical prostatectomy. CT abdomen/pelvis and a bone scan are both normal. Which imaging test is most likely to localise recurrent disease?
options: Repeat CT with contrast in 6 months
PSMA PET/CT
Transrectal ultrasound of the prostate bed
Plain radiograph of the pelvis
FDG PET/CT
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: PSMA PET/CT
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: PSMA PET/CT detects recurrent prostate cancer at low PSA levels where CT and bone scan are typically negative. Its high tumour-to-background contrast localises small nodal and bone deposits, directing salvage therapy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which of the following is a recognised cause of a false-negative PSMA PET scan in a patient with active prostate cancer?
options: Physiological salivary gland uptake
Excreted tracer in the bladder
A dedifferentiated neuroendocrine tumour with low PSMA expression
Uptake in a coeliac ganglion
Renal cortical uptake
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A dedifferentiated neuroendocrine tumour with low PSMA expression
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Dedifferentiated and neuroendocrine prostate tumours may express little or no PSMA, so they can fail to accumulate tracer despite active disease. This is why a negative scan does not exclude cancer and must be read alongside PSA kinetics.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which structure represents normal physiological uptake on PSMA PET rather than metastatic disease?
options: A focal deposit in the L3 vertebral body
An enlarged avid external iliac lymph node
The salivary glands
A soft-tissue nodule in the prostate bed
An avid rib lesion at a non-fracture site
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: The salivary glands
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: The salivary and lacrimal glands normally show intense physiological PSMA uptake and should not be mistaken for disease. Recognising this pattern, along with renal and bowel activity, is essential for accurate reporting.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 58-year-old with biopsy-proven metastatic well-differentiated ileal NET is referred for ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT. He receives monthly long-acting lanreotide, with his last dose 5 days ago. What is the most appropriate advice regarding timing?
options: Proceed immediately; depot analogues do not affect the scan
Delay the scan and perform it just before the next depot dose is due
Give an extra subcutaneous octreotide dose on the morning of the scan
Stop all analgesia and fast for 12 hours before imaging
Switch the study to an FDG-PET instead
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Delay the scan and perform it just before the next depot dose is due
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Somatostatin analogues compete with the tracer for SSTR2 and can produce false-negative studies. Scanning at the trough, just before the next depot injection, minimises receptor blockade and maximises tumour uptake.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which structure demonstrates physiological ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE uptake that is a well-recognised cause of a false-positive for a pancreatic NET?
options: Gallbladder fundus
Uncinate process of the pancreas
Second part of the duodenum
Portal vein
Left adrenal medulla only
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Uncinate process of the pancreas
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: The uncinate process normally accumulates tracer and is a classic pseudolesion mimicking a pancreatic NET. Correlation with the CT component and lesion morphology distinguishes physiology from a true tumour.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with a known NET has a lesion that is intensely FDG-avid but shows no uptake on ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT. What does this pattern most likely indicate?
options: A benign lipoma
A well-differentiated, low-grade tumour ideal for PRRT
A poorly-differentiated, high-grade lesion with loss of somatostatin receptors
A technical artefact from renal tracer excretion
Physiological splenic uptake
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A poorly-differentiated, high-grade lesion with loss of somatostatin receptors
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: As NETs dedifferentiate they lose SSTR expression and gain glucose metabolism, becoming FDG-avid but DOTATATE-negative. Such high-grade lesions carry a worse prognosis and are unsuitable for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A whole-body ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP bone scan shows diffuse, intense uptake throughout the axial skeleton with virtually no visible kidney or bladder activity. What does this pattern represent?
options: Normal physiological distribution
Superscan from widespread osteoblastic metastases
Technical failure of the gamma camera
Free ⁹⁹ᵐTc pertechnetate contamination
Renal tract obstruction
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Superscan from widespread osteoblastic metastases
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A superscan shows avid, uniform skeletal uptake so that almost all injected tracer is bound to bone, leaving the kidneys and bladder faint or 'absent'. It reflects diffuse osteoblastic metastatic disease (or metabolic bone disease) and is a classic exam sign.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with right-upper-quadrant pain has a HIDA scan. At 60 minutes there is good hepatic uptake and tracer in the duodenum, but the gallbladder is not visualised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Common bile duct obstruction
Biliary atresia
Acute cholecystitis from cystic duct obstruction
Bile leak
Normal study
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Acute cholecystitis from cystic duct obstruction
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Non-filling of the gallbladder at 60 minutes despite tracer reaching the bowel indicates cystic duct obstruction, the hallmark of acute cholecystitis. Passage into the duodenum confirms the common bile duct is patent, localising the block to the cystic duct.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which statement about radiation safety for a ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP bone scan is correct?
options: Thyroid blockade with potassium iodide is mandatory beforehand
Breastfeeding can continue without any interruption
Patients should drink fluids and void frequently afterwards to reduce bladder dose
It delivers a higher dose than whole-body PET/CT
Iodinated contrast nephrotoxicity is the main concern
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Patients should drink fluids and void frequently afterwards to reduce bladder dose
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: MDP is renally excreted, so hydration and frequent voiding clear tracer from the bladder and lower the gonadal and bladder radiation dose. ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP needs no thyroid blockade and involves no iodinated contrast.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 74-year-old man with HFpEF and unexplained LV wall thickening has a ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DPD scan showing myocardial uptake equal to rib uptake (Perugini grade 2). His serum free light chains, serum immunofixation and urine immunofixation are all normal. What is the most appropriate diagnostic conclusion?
options: Diagnose ATTR cardiac amyloidosis without endomyocardial biopsy
Diagnose AL cardiac amyloidosis and start chemotherapy
Proceed to endomyocardial biopsy to confirm the diagnosis
The scan is negative; amyloidosis is excluded
Repeat the scan in 12 months before deciding
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Diagnose ATTR cardiac amyloidosis without endomyocardial biopsy
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A Perugini grade 2–3 scan combined with a negative monoclonal protein screen is over 99% specific for ATTR. This validated non-biopsy pathway allows a confident diagnosis without endomyocardial biopsy. Genotyping then separates hereditary from wild-type ATTR.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Why is a serum free light chain assay with serum and urine immunofixation mandatory alongside a positive bone scan?
options: To exclude AL amyloidosis, which can also show tracer uptake and requires urgent haematology treatment
To confirm the tracer was injected intravenously rather than subcutaneously
To calculate the correct radiation dose for the study
To determine whether SPECT rather than planar imaging is needed
To assess renal function before tracer administration
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: To exclude AL amyloidosis, which can also show tracer uptake and requires urgent haematology treatment
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: AL amyloid occasionally produces myocardial tracer uptake, so a positive scan is not specific on its own. A negative monoclonal screen rules out AL, which is a haematological emergency needing prompt treatment. Only then can the scan be attributed to ATTR.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which finding on a bone-avid tracer study is regarded as POSITIVE for cardiac ATTR amyloidosis?
options: Perugini grade 2–3 myocardial uptake (cardiac uptake equal to or greater than bone)
Perugini grade 0 with normal skeletal uptake
Grade 1 uptake, less than bone, on planar imaging only
Tracer confined to the blood pool on early imaging
A heart:contralateral ratio of 0.8 at one hour
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Perugini grade 2–3 myocardial uptake (cardiac uptake equal to or greater than bone)
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Grade 2 (cardiac equal to bone) and grade 3 (cardiac greater than bone with reduced skeletal signal) are the positive categories. A supportive heart:contralateral ratio is 1.5 or higher at one hour. SPECT confirms the uptake is truly myocardial.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A diabetic patient has focal increased uptake on the flow, blood-pool AND delayed images of a three-phase bone scan of the foot. What does this pattern most support?
options: Cellulitis with no bone involvement
Osteomyelitis
Normal physiological skeletal uptake
Deep vein thrombosis
Resolved previous infection
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Osteomyelitis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Positivity in all three phases indicates increased blood flow, soft-tissue hyperaemia and, critically, osteoblastic bone uptake. This triad is the classic scintigraphic pattern of osteomyelitis.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: In three-phase bone scintigraphy, which phase best distinguishes osteomyelitis from cellulitis?
options: The flow/angiographic phase
The blood-pool phase
The delayed (2–4h) bone phase
The excretory renal phase
The equilibrium cardiac phase
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: The delayed (2–4h) bone phase
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Cellulitis increases the flow and blood-pool phases but shows no focal delayed uptake because bone is not involved. Focal uptake on the delayed bone phase indicates true osteoblastic bone infection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which agent is used to improve specificity for infection when a three-phase bone scan is positive near recent surgery or metalwork?
options: ¹²³I-labelled iodide
⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled white cells (HMPAO leucocytes)
¹⁸F-FDG for viability only
⁹⁹ᵐTc-sestamibi for parathyroid
⁶⁷Ga-citrate for tumour staging only
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled white cells (HMPAO leucocytes)
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Labelled white-cell scanning (⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO or ¹¹¹In-oxine leucocytes) accumulates at sites of active infection rather than bland bone remodelling. It is the standard adjunct where bone turnover is already raised by surgery, fracture or hardware.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with a dilated left pelvicalyceal system undergoes a MAG3 renogram. The left curve rises steadily and does not fall; after IV frusemide there is still no washout. What does this indicate?
options: A baggy, non-obstructed collecting system
True mechanical obstruction
Normal renal drainage
Acute tubular necrosis
Renal artery stenosis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: True mechanical obstruction
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A curve that keeps rising and fails to wash out after a diuretic challenge is the hallmark of genuine obstruction. The diuretic forces a high urine flow, so a truly obstructed system cannot drain and retains tracer.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Why is ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAG3 generally preferred over ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA for dynamic renography?
options: It is filtered rather than secreted
It contains iodine for better contrast
It is tubularly secreted with high extraction, giving better images in poor function
It delivers no radiation dose
It is the only agent measuring split function
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: It is tubularly secreted with high extraction, giving better images in poor function
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: MAG3 is actively secreted by the proximal tubules and has a high extraction fraction, producing superior image quality. This advantage is greatest in kidneys with impaired function, where DTPA's filtered images are poor.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which additional agent is administered during renography to investigate renovascular hypertension from renal artery stenosis?
options: Frusemide
Captopril
Iodinated contrast
Potassium perchlorate
Adenosine
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Captopril
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Captopril is an ACE inhibitor that removes efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, unmasking a functionally significant renal artery stenosis. The stenosed kidney's renogram curve deteriorates after captopril compared with baseline.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which cellular process explains the renal localisation of ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DMSA?
options: Glomerular filtration with rapid tubular excretion
Binding and retention within proximal tubular cells of the cortex
Active secretion into the collecting ducts
Uptake by medullary loops of Henle
Sequestration by renal macrophages
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Binding and retention within proximal tubular cells of the cortex
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: DMSA is bound and fixed in proximal tubular cells, so it accumulates in and marks functioning cortex. This cortical retention with minimal excretion is what makes it ideal for scar detection and split function.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A child has a DMSA scan showing a focal cold cortical defect with a preserved renal outline and no volume loss. What is the most likely interpretation?
options: Established cortical scar
Acute pyelonephritis
Duplex collecting system
Renal cell carcinoma
Normal variant of uptake
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Acute pyelonephritis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Acute pyelonephritis produces photopenic defects while the renal outline and volume are preserved. A scar, by contrast, shows volume loss and cortical thinning.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: When is imaging typically performed after intravenous injection of ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DMSA?
options: Immediately during first-pass perfusion
At 15–20 minutes
At 2–4 hours
At 24 hours
At 72 hours
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: At 2–4 hours
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Imaging at 2–4 hours allows cortical fixation of the tracer and clearance of background activity. This delay gives the clean static cortical images DMSA is valued for.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 40-year-old woman with a suppressed TSH and raised free T4 has thyroid scintigraphy showing diffuse, homogeneously increased uptake throughout an enlarged gland. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Graves' disease
Toxic adenoma
De Quervain's thyroiditis
Factitious thyrotoxicosis
Papillary carcinoma
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Graves' disease
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Diffuse, homogeneously increased uptake across the whole enlarged gland is the classic scintigraphic pattern of Graves' disease. The autoantibody-driven stimulation activates the entire gland uniformly.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient booked for ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate thyroid scintigraphy had a contrast-enhanced CT with iodinated contrast three days ago. Why should the scan be deferred?
options: The iodine load saturates the sodium-iodide symporter and blunts tracer uptake
Iodinated contrast reacts chemically with technetium
Contrast causes the thyroid to organify pertechnetate
The contrast increases the radiation dose to unsafe levels
Iodinated contrast triggers a hypersensitivity reaction to the tracer
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: The iodine load saturates the sodium-iodide symporter and blunts tracer uptake
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Recent iodinated contrast delivers a large iodine load that competes at the sodium-iodide symporter, producing falsely low uptake and an uninterpretable scan. Imaging is deferred until the iodine load clears.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Thyroid scintigraphy of a solitary palpable nodule shows the nodule as an area of absent tracer uptake (a 'cold' nodule). What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration
Reassure and discharge as this indicates a benign adenoma
Immediate total thyroidectomy
Radioiodine ablation therapy
Start carbimazole
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A cold nodule is hypofunctioning and carries a slightly increased risk of malignancy compared with a hot nodule. It warrants fine-needle aspiration cytology to characterise it.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 34-year-old woman with thyrotoxicosis undergoes a radioactive iodine uptake scan, which shows markedly reduced, near-absent uptake throughout the gland. Which diagnosis does this pattern best support?
options: Graves' disease
Toxic multinodular goitre
Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis
Solitary toxic adenoma
Retrosternal functioning goitre
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Thyroiditis causes thyrotoxicosis from release of preformed hormone by damaged follicles, so trapping of new iodine falls and uptake is low. Graves' and toxic nodular disease both drive active hormone synthesis and therefore show high uptake.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which statement about ¹³¹I radioiodine therapy is correct?
options: It is safe to administer during the first trimester of pregnancy
Its beta emission delivers a local ablative dose to functioning thyroid tissue
Breastfeeding may continue normally during treatment
It is the treatment of choice for thyrotoxicosis due to thyroiditis
A low-iodine diet reduces its effectiveness and should be avoided
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Its beta emission delivers a local ablative dose to functioning thyroid tissue
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: ¹³¹I emits beta particles that are concentrated by functioning cells and destroy them locally, making it effective for Graves', toxic nodules and thyroid cancer. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are absolute contraindications, and thyroiditis has low uptake so radioiodine is ineffective.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A woman is scheduled for ¹³¹I ablation after total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma. Which pre-treatment step maximises iodine uptake by residual thyroid tissue?
options: Administering iodinated CT contrast the day before
Starting a high-iodine diet with kelp supplements
Continuing amiodarone throughout treatment
A low-iodine diet with stimulation by thyroid hormone withdrawal or rhTSH
Giving a saturated solution of potassium iodide beforehand
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A low-iodine diet with stimulation by thyroid hormone withdrawal or rhTSH
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Depleting the body iodine pool with a low-iodine diet increases avidity for the radioiodine, and raising TSH by hormone withdrawal or recombinant TSH (rhTSH) stimulates NIS-mediated uptake. Iodine loads such as contrast, kelp, amiodarone or potassium iodide saturate the gland and block uptake.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A thyroid nodule FNA is reported as Thy3f (follicular neoplasm). What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure and discharge the patient
Repeat the fine-needle aspiration in 6 months
Diagnostic hemithyroidectomy
Start levothyroxine suppression therapy
Radioactive iodine ablation
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Diagnostic hemithyroidectomy
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Thy3f indicates a follicular neoplasm, but cytology cannot distinguish a benign adenoma from a carcinoma because that requires assessment of capsular/vascular invasion. Diagnostic hemithyroidectomy provides the capsule histology needed to make that distinction.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A thyroid nodule FNA yields an inadequate sample reported as Thy1. What is the correct next step?
options: Proceed directly to total thyroidectomy
Repeat the ultrasound-guided FNA
Reassure the patient that the nodule is benign
Commence carbimazole
Arrange radioiodine therapy
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Repeat the ultrasound-guided FNA
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Thy1 means the aspirate was non-diagnostic or inadequate and yields no information about malignancy risk. The appropriate action is to repeat the FNA under ultrasound guidance, targeting any solid component to improve cellular yield.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which feature on thyroid ultrasound most strongly suggests malignancy and would prompt FNA?
options: Peripheral eggshell calcification
Spongiform (honeycomb) appearance
A complete peripheral hypoechoic halo
Punctate microcalcification with a taller-than-wide shape
A purely anechoic simple cyst
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Punctate microcalcification with a taller-than-wide shape
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Punctate microcalcification and a taller-than-wide (anteroposterior greater than transverse) shape are classic U4/U5 sonographic features of malignancy, particularly papillary carcinoma. These indeterminate-to-suspicious features are the ones that select a nodule for FNA.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which property must an isotope GFR tracer such as ⁵¹Cr-EDTA possess for its plasma clearance to equal the GFR?
options: It is freely filtered but not secreted or reabsorbed by the tubules
It is actively secreted by the proximal tubule
It is highly protein-bound in plasma
It is partially reabsorbed in the distal tubule
It is metabolised by the renal parenchyma
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: It is freely filtered but not secreted or reabsorbed by the tubules
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A valid GFR marker crosses the glomerular filter freely and is neither secreted nor reabsorbed, so filtration is its only route of clearance. This makes its plasma clearance a direct measure of glomerular filtration rate.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 62-year-old woman needs carboplatin chemotherapy dosed by the Calvert formula. Why is an isotope GFR requested rather than relying on creatinine-based eGFR?
options: It provides an accurate measured GFR needed for safe carboplatin dosing
It measures renal blood flow rather than filtration
It avoids any radiation exposure to the patient
It is quicker and needs no blood sampling
It quantifies tubular secretory capacity
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: It provides an accurate measured GFR needed for safe carboplatin dosing
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Carboplatin is dosed by the Calvert formula, dose = AUC × (GFR + 25), so an inaccurate GFR risks toxicity or underdosing. Isotope GFR directly measures filtration and is the reference standard when precision matters.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: During an isotope GFR study, which factor most threatens the accuracy of the calculated result?
options: Marked extracellular fluid overload with ascites and oedema
The patient having a normal serum creatinine
Use of the opposite arm for venous sampling
Reporting the result corrected to body surface area
A low background radiation dose from the tracer
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Marked extracellular fluid overload with ascites and oedema
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: In gross ECF expansion the tracer distributes into the enlarged fluid compartment and equilibrates slowly, distorting the clearance curve. Extended or multi-sample protocols are needed to obtain a reliable value in these patients.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 27-year-old pregnant woman has suspected PE and a normal chest X-ray. Which V/Q finding would most strongly indicate pulmonary embolism?
options: Matched ventilation and perfusion defects in the right base
A segmental perfusion defect with preserved ventilation in the same region
Uniformly reduced ventilation across both lungs
A normal perfusion scan with a small ventilation defect
Increased perfusion to the upper zones
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A segmental perfusion defect with preserved ventilation in the same region
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: PE occludes a pulmonary artery, abolishing perfusion while ventilation to that segment remains intact. This perfusion–ventilation mismatch is the diagnostic hallmark of pulmonary embolism.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which radiopharmaceutical is injected intravenously for the perfusion component of a V/Q scan, and how does it localise?
options: ⁸¹ᵐKr gas that fills the alveoli
⁹⁹ᵐTc-Technegas inhaled into the airways
⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAA particles that lodge in pulmonary capillaries
¹²³I that concentrates in thyroid tissue
¹⁸F-FDG taken up by metabolically active cells
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAA particles that lodge in pulmonary capillaries
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Macroaggregated albumin particles are large enough to microembolise and lodge in the pulmonary capillary bed after IV injection, mapping regional blood flow. Only a tiny fraction of capillaries is occluded, so the study is safe.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: In which patient is a V/Q scan the most appropriate first-line investigation for suspected PE?
options: A patient whose chest X-ray shows dense right lower lobe consolidation
A young woman with a normal chest X-ray and a documented severe iodinated contrast allergy
A patient with a large right-to-left cardiac shunt
A patient with extensive bilateral pulmonary oedema on CXR
A patient with a known allergy to macroaggregated albumin
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A young woman with a normal chest X-ray and a documented severe iodinated contrast allergy
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A V/Q scan avoids iodinated contrast and spares breast radiation, making it ideal when CTPA is contraindicated. A normal chest X-ray maximises specificity, giving the most interpretable result.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient undergoes SPECT MPI. The inferior wall shows reduced tracer uptake on the stress images but normal uptake on the rest images. What does this pattern indicate?
options: Inducible ischaemia in the inferior (RCA) territory
Full-thickness infarct of the inferior wall
Non-viable scar tissue
A normal study with no significant coronary disease
Artefact from breast attenuation
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Inducible ischaemia in the inferior (RCA) territory
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A defect that is abnormal on stress but normalises at rest is a reversible defect, the signature of inducible ischaemia from a flow-limiting stenosis. The inferior wall corresponds to the right coronary artery territory. The myocardium is viable, which is why perfusion recovers at rest.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which instruction is essential before pharmacological stress MPI using adenosine?
options: Withhold caffeine and theophylline for at least 12–24 hours beforehand
Load with a beta-blocker on the morning of the test
Administer thyroid blockade with potassium iodide the day before
Give prophylactic salbutamol nebuliser to all patients
Fast the patient for 6 hours to reduce bowel tracer uptake
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Withhold caffeine and theophylline for at least 12–24 hours beforehand
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Caffeine and theophylline are competitive adenosine-receptor antagonists that blunt the vasodilator response and cause false-negative studies. They must be stopped for around 12–24 hours before adenosine or dipyridamole stress. This preparation preserves the sensitivity of the test for detecting ischaemia.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with brittle asthma needs a functional test for suspected coronary disease and cannot exercise. Which stress method is most appropriate?
options: Dobutamine stress
Adenosine infusion
Dipyridamole infusion
Regadenoson bolus
Standard treadmill exercise
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Dobutamine stress
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Adenosine, dipyridamole and regadenoson are vasodilators that can precipitate bronchospasm and are contraindicated in significant asthma. Dobutamine works by increasing myocardial oxygen demand through inotropy and chronotropy, avoiding adenosine-receptor stimulation. It is the preferred pharmacological stressor when the patient cannot exercise and vasodilators are unsafe.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with biochemically confirmed phaeochromocytoma is booked for a 123I-MIBG scan. Which preparation is essential to protect a specific organ from the radiopharmaceutical?
options: Potassium iodide (thyroid blockade) before and after the scan
Intravenous N-acetylcysteine to protect the kidneys
Oral bicarbonate loading to protect the bladder
Corticosteroid premedication to protect the adrenal cortex
Prophylactic amiodarone to protect the myocardium
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Potassium iodide (thyroid blockade) before and after the scan
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: MIBG is labelled with radioiodine, and free radioiodine is concentrated by the thyroid. Potassium iodide or Lugol's iodine saturates the thyroid so it cannot take up the radioiodine, shielding it from radiation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: An MIBG scan for suspected phaeochromocytoma is reported as negative despite convincing biochemistry. Which of the patient's medications is the most likely cause of a false-negative result?
options: Labetalol
Amoxicillin
Paracetamol
Omeprazole
Levothyroxine
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Labetalol
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Labetalol is a combined alpha/beta blocker that interferes with MIBG uptake and storage at the noradrenaline transporter. Failing to withhold it can produce a false-negative scan, so it must be stopped for an appropriate washout period.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which finding on a 24-hour MIBG scan represents normal physiological uptake rather than tumour?
options: Activity in the salivary glands, myocardium, liver and bladder
A discrete focus of uptake in a lumbar vertebral body
Multiple foci of uptake throughout the axial skeleton
Intense focal uptake in an enlarged extra-adrenal soft-tissue mass
A rim of uptake around a liver metastasis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Activity in the salivary glands, myocardium, liver and bladder
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Salivary glands, myocardium, liver, spleen, bowel and the urinary tract show expected physiological MIBG uptake. Uptake in bone, discrete masses or nodal deposits outside these sites indicates tumour.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A DaTscan (¹²³I-ioflupane SPECT) primarily images the integrity of which structure?
options: Postsynaptic dopamine D2 receptors
The presynaptic dopamine transporter on nigrostriatal terminals
Striatal glucose metabolism
Amyloid plaque burden in the cortex
Cerebral blood flow in the basal ganglia
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: The presynaptic dopamine transporter on nigrostriatal terminals
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Ioflupane is a cocaine analogue that binds the presynaptic dopamine transporter (DAT) on dopaminergic terminals in the striatum. Loss of tracer signal reflects loss of these presynaptic terminals, marking a true nigrostriatal degeneration.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 62-year-old has an asymmetric tremor and rigidity. A DaTscan shows reduced striatal uptake with loss of the putaminal tail. What does this reliably indicate?
options: Parkinson's disease specifically, excluding MSA and PSP
Essential tremor
A presynaptic dopaminergic deficit consistent with a degenerative parkinsonian syndrome
Drug-induced parkinsonism
Alzheimer's disease
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A presynaptic dopaminergic deficit consistent with a degenerative parkinsonian syndrome
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Reduced, asymmetric striatal uptake confirms a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit. This pattern is shared by Parkinson's disease, MSA and PSP, so it establishes degeneration without identifying the specific syndrome.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which preparation step is specifically required before administering ¹²³I-ioflupane?
options: Loading with intravenous levodopa
Thyroid blockade with potassium iodide
Fasting for 12 hours
Prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics
Bowel preparation with an osmotic laxative
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Thyroid blockade with potassium iodide
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Free radioiodide (¹²³I⁻) released from the tracer concentrates in the thyroid, so potassium iodide is given to saturate and protect the gland. Drugs affecting DAT binding are also withheld, but thyroid blockade is the isotope-specific requirement.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 68-year-old with recurrent obscure PR bleeding has negative OGD and colonoscopy. Labelled RBC scintigraphy is requested. Which radiopharmaceutical is used?
options: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled autologous red blood cells
⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate (free)
¹⁸F-FDG
⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP
⁶⁷Ga-citrate
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled autologous red blood cells
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Labelled RBC scintigraphy tags the patient's own red cells with ⁹⁹ᵐTc so they remain in the vascular pool. A leak into the bowel lumen then shows as an abnormal focus of extravasated activity.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: On a dynamic labelled RBC study, which finding confirms active gastrointestinal bleeding?
options: A focus of activity that appears and migrates along the bowel with peristalsis
Symmetrical activity in both kidneys
Persistent uniform blood-pool activity in the great vessels
A fixed focus over the cardiac blood pool
Diffuse activity in the urinary bladder
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A focus of activity that appears and migrates along the bowel with peristalsis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: True luminal bleeding produces a focus that increases in intensity and moves along the bowel over sequential frames. Fixed vascular or excreted activity is expected normal biodistribution.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 3-year-old boy presents with painless rectal bleeding. Which scan and tracer best identifies the likely cause?
options: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate Meckel's scan detecting ectopic gastric mucosa
⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled RBC scan for slow venous ooze
⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO white-cell scan
¹²³I-MIBG scan
⁹⁹ᵐTc-DMSA renal scan
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate Meckel's scan detecting ectopic gastric mucosa
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Painless PR bleeding in a young child suggests a Meckel's diverticulum containing ectopic gastric mucosa. Free ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate is concentrated by that mucosa, producing a focus in the right lower quadrant.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with a painful hip prosthesis and raised inflammatory markers has an equivocal MRI degraded by metal artefact. Which combination best confirms or excludes prosthetic joint infection?
options: Labelled white cell scan combined with a ⁹⁹ᵐTc bone marrow scan
⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP three-phase bone scan alone
¹⁸F-FDG PET brain scan
⁹⁹ᵐTc-DMSA renal scan
V/Q perfusion lung scan
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Labelled white cell scan combined with a ⁹⁹ᵐTc bone marrow scan
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Labelled leucocytes accumulate at sites of active infection, and the marrow scan distinguishes true infection from physiological marrow uptake. Infection is shown by white-cell uptake that is not matched on the marrow map, which maximises specificity around a prosthesis.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: On serial imaging, which finding on a labelled white cell scan most strongly indicates active infection?
options: A focus of uptake that increases in intensity and extent between early and delayed images
Intense uptake confined to the spleen
Uptake in liver and bone marrow only
A focus that fades in intensity on delayed images
Diffuse blood-pool activity that clears uniformly
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A focus of uptake that increases in intensity and extent between early and delayed images
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Ongoing recruitment of labelled neutrophils to an infective focus causes uptake to rise over time. Physiological splenic, hepatic and marrow activity form the expected normal distribution, and a fading focus argues against infection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which radiopharmaceutical is preferred for a labelled white cell scan investigating a suspected intra-abdominal collection because it shows no physiological bowel excretion?
options: ¹¹¹In-oxine labelled leucocytes
⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO labelled leucocytes
⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAG3
⁹⁹ᵐTc-sestamibi
¹²³I-MIBG
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: ¹¹¹In-oxine labelled leucocytes
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: ¹¹¹In-oxine provides a very stable intracellular label with no bowel or urinary excretion, so abdominal foci are not obscured by physiological gut activity. ⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO shows delayed bowel, urinary and gallbladder clearance that can confound abdominal interpretation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A woman with early invasive breast cancer and a clinically node-negative axilla undergoes sentinel lymph node biopsy. What is the principal benefit of this approach compared with routine axillary clearance?
options: It delivers a higher radiation dose to sterilise tumour cells
It avoids the morbidity of full axillary dissection, chiefly lymphoedema, when the node is negative
It removes the need for any histological examination of nodes
It replaces the need for adjuvant systemic therapy
It guarantees no further surgery will ever be required
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: It avoids the morbidity of full axillary dissection, chiefly lymphoedema, when the node is negative
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A negative sentinel node reliably predicts a tumour-free basin, so completion axillary dissection can be safely omitted. This spares the patient the lymphoedema, nerve injury and shoulder morbidity of full clearance, which is the central rationale for SLNB.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which agent is injected around the tumour to localise the sentinel node on lymphoscintigraphy?
options: Iodinated CT contrast medium
Gadolinium-based contrast agent
⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled nanocolloid
¹⁸F-fluorodeoxyglucose
Barium sulphate suspension
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled nanocolloid
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-nanocolloid particles are small enough to enter lymphatics and are trapped in the first draining node, marking it as a focal hot spot. The node is then found with a gamma probe at surgery, often alongside blue dye.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: During a sentinel node biopsy the patient becomes hypotensive with a fall in measured oxygen saturation shortly after the intra-operative dye is given. Which agent is the most likely cause?
options: Patent blue dye
⁹⁹ᵐTc-nanocolloid radiotracer
Normal saline flush
Local anaesthetic infiltration
The gamma probe's contact gel
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Patent blue dye
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Patent blue dye carries a recognised risk of anaphylaxis, presenting with hypotension and cardiovascular collapse. It also causes an artefactual drop in pulse-oximetry readings, so the anaesthetist should be forewarned before it is injected.
